title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Pulse-check decisions
Learners will practice:

Preparing a pulse check before the pause
Making a shock/no-shock call under uncertainty
Preventing airway/procedure pauses
Using EtCO2 and other signals when ROSC is uncertain

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Code blue on E50
Compressions are ongoing when you arrive.
You establish yourself as code leader.
Prompt: You have 20 seconds before the next pulse check. What do you assign?

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Before the pause
Try:

“Recorder, call out pause time.”


“You check pulse.”


“You call rhythm.”


“Defib team, be ready if shockable.”


“Everyone else: compressions resume unless I say shock.”

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
First pulse check
No palpable pulse

Shock, no shock, or uncertain?Prompt: Shock, no shock, or uncertain?

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Fine VF vs asystole


If uncertain:

Turn up gain.
Check leads/connection.
Voice your uncertainty.
If it could be VF/pVT, shock (consider consequences of each error).
If not, resume CPR.





Coarse vs fine ventricular fibrillation

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Second pulse check
No palpable pulse

Airway team ready to intubate, asks for a moment before resuming compressionsPrompt: What is the rhythm now, and what do you do about the airway request?

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Airway answer
Answer:

“Airway, keep working during compressions. We’ll give you the next planned pause only if you are ready.”


“If intubation will interrupt CPR, put in an LMA.”

Airway does not own the pause.

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
What really matters
During arrest, protect two things:

Compression fraction
Early defibrillation for shockable rhythm

Everything else has to fit around those.

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Confirming ROSC can be hard
Consider the consequences of each error.
Use:

EtCO2 trend or sudden rise
Arterial line or pleth waveform if present
Doppler if ready
POCUS only if pre-positioned
Clinical signs

When in doubt, continue compressions.
No probe fishing during pulse checks.

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
section: EtCO2 is a cue, not proof
text:
EtCO2 is a cue, not proof

Use EtCO2 to help detect ROSCEtCO2 is a cue, not proof; if unclear, continue CPR.

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Third pulse check

EtCO2 = 36 mmHgPrompt: What do you say?
Suggested answer:

“Possible ROSC. At the next check: rhythm, pulse, waveform. If not convincing, resume compressions.”

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Make uncertainty public and brief
Name what is uncertain, then name the action.
Try:

Fine VF vs asystole: gain/leads now; if still possibly VF/pVT, shock.
Possible ROSC: rhythm, pulse, waveform; if unclear, CPR continues.
Disagreement on pulse: compressions continue while we clarify.

title: Pulse Checks: The 10-Second Decision
text:
Summary
Do not miss fine VF.
Do not prolong pauses for procedures.
Do not keep uncertainty private.
Use EtCO2 to monitor compressions and help detect ROSC.

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Leadership in the first 60 seconds
Learners will practice:

Naming who is leading
Anchoring the room
Making the working problem and plan public
Inviting concern before action

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Case start
Rapid response to S408
Sign-out: “81M, SVT, now stable.”
Now: HR 160, MAP 85 -> 70, lightheaded.
A bedside nurse says: “He looks worse than he did 10 minutes ago.”
Prompt: Before choosing a medication, what do you say to the room?

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Say the sentence
Try:

“I’m [name], the senior medicine resident responding to the rapid. Who is currently coordinating this response?”

Then choose:

“Okay, I’ll run the room.”


“Can I take over?”


“Okay, how can I help?”

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Failure mode
Ways this commonly goes wrong:

Multiple teams entered.
No one named who owned the response.
The resident’s plan and the primary/CV plan diverged.
A medication order lacked clear dose, owner, and readback.
The nurse’s clarification was the safety signal.

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Anchor the room
If you are leading:

Stay visible and findable.
Delegate tasks by name or function.
Keep patient, monitor, nurse, doorway, and task flow in view.


“I’m staying here to run the room; bring questions or data to me.”

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Make the plan public
Try:

“I think [problem] is the issue. I’m worried about [risk]. My plan is [plan].”

Then ask:

“What are we missing?”

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Invite expertise without losing leadership

Bedside nurse: what changed?
Outreach nurse: biggest worry?
Pharmacy: dose and contraindications?

Leadership is keeping the plan public, not proving you can do tasks yourself.

title: Leadership in the First 60 Seconds
text:
Summary
Four moves

Name the leadership state.
Anchor yourself.
Say the working problem and first plan.
Invite concern before action.

Next: apply the same leadership clarity to pulse-check decisions. The nurse-response module later builds on this language for bedside and outreach collaboration.

title: Case 4
text:
Case 4
36F admitted for ETOH detox.
RRT activated on third day of admission.
Tachycardic, HR 180s, dizzy/lightheaded but responsive, pulsatile in all ext.

title: Case 4
text:
Team interface prompt
The outreach nurse arrived before you and has already tried vagal maneuvers.
Start with:

“Can I get the 30-second story: what changed, what have you tried, and what are you worried about?”

Then state whether this is stable, unstable, or peri-arrest.

Peri-Adenosine EKG:

Vagal maneuvers tried, then adenosine given. What’s this rhythm?

title: Case 4

title: Case 4
text:
Teaching Points

Adenosine is for stable, regular, monomorphic tachycardia when SVT or regular monomorphic WCT is possible. Do not give it for unstable, irregular, or polymorphic WCT.
If the rhythm is narrow and fast, decide whether it is causing instability or reflecting another problem.

title: Case 2
text:
Case 2
58F with history of CAD s/p multiple remote DES, HLD, T2DM, Active smoker now admitted for UTI with sepsis.
Telemetry alarms “code blue” on hospital day 2.
On initial assessment, pulses are absent.

title: Case 2

Labs

Acid-base: pH 7.18, HCO₃⁻ 16, pCO₂ 48.
Perfusion/electrolytes: lactate 6.5, K⁺ 4.9, iCa²⁺ 1.10.
Context: glucose 152, hs-TnI 121 (ULN 50).

title: Case 2
text: Rhythm Check

Post-ROSC EKG

Next step?

title: Case 2
section: After ROSC: stabilize before you celebrate
text:
After ROSC: stabilize before you celebrate

ECG as soon as feasible.
O2 100% until reliable; then SpO2 90-98%.
PaCO2 35-45 if comatose/ventilated.
Avoid hypotension; MAP >=65.
If unresponsive: temperature control >=36 hours.
Search cause: coronary, PE, tamponade, hemorrhage, PTX, tox/metabolic.

title: Case 2
text:
Team interface prompt
The nurse who called the code saw the telemetry alarm and knows when the patient lost pulses.
Ask:

“What rhythm triggered the alarm, when did compressions start, and has the first shock happened?”

Close the loop on shock timing and post-ROSC ECG.

title: Case 2
text:
Teaching Points

Time to first shock is critical in VF
Role of antiarrhythmics is adjunctive, not primary
Persisting VF/pVT: follow device energy strategy; if unsure, maximum biphasic energy is reasonable. Protect compression fraction and confirm pads/contact. Do not teach routine DSED/vector-change as standard care.
VF/VT: Think.. acute MI (sudden, chest pain), electrolyte derangements, drug toxicity

title: Case 2
text:
Case summary
Label: VF/VT arrest with post-ROSC ECG and stabilization.
Key issue: shock early, protect compression fraction, then stabilize and search for the post-ROSC cause.

text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of the session, learners should be able to:

Make the leadership state clear on arrival: lead, support, consult, or transition leadership explicitly.
Prepare pulse checks, make shock/no-shock decisions public, and protect compression pauses.
Use bedside nurse and outreach trajectory to identify key decisions, needed resources, and the next-step plan.
Decide what next care step the patient needs and activate the appropriate site-specific resource or destination.
Close each rapid/code with explicit disposition, follow-up owner, callback plan, family plan when needed, and debrief.







Tip



Didactics alone have limits. Regular review, simulation, interprofessional practice, and feedback after real events are what turn these skills into reflexes.

title: 2026 Code Blue and Rapid Response Seminar
text:
Why This Course Exists
Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership is not just algorithm recall. The resident leader has to make the room work: make the leadership state explicit, make roles visible, keep communication psychologically safe, integrate bedside expertise, and escalate resources before the response stalls.
Stakeholders from Code Blue and Rapid Response teams, including senior residents, nurses, respiratory therapists, and quality leads, identified four recurring hazards during resident-led responses:

Unclear team leadership, which can cause role confusion, low psychological safety, and decreased collaboration. (Steinbach et al. 2024)
Failure to cardiovert or defibrillate shockable rhythms.
Delayed critical decisions, including calling for help, initial stabilization, and transport to ICU.
Poorly defined collaboration between residents and bedside nurses, nurse-led rapid response teams, or critical care outreach teams.

This seminar targets those hazards through brief micro-skills, discussion, hands-on scenarios, and interprofessional scripts that can be used during real events.

title: Resources
text: Quick reference materials for Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership.

title: Resources
text:
Key Points

Name the leadership state early. Ask who is coordinating, then lead, support, consult, or transition leadership explicitly.
Get the nursing trajectory. Ask bedside and outreach nurses what changed, what has been tried, and what worries them most.
Protect pulse checks. Prepare the pause, make shock/no-shock and pulse/no-pulse decisions public, and resume compressions quickly when uncertain.
Plan the next step explicitly. Use bedside and outreach expertise to identify the key decision, needed resource, destination, and trigger.
Close the loop before leaving. Name disposition, follow-up owner, callback person, and the trigger for calling RRT, ICU, or code response.

title: Case 3
text:
Learning Points

Sustained polymorphic VT is unstable: shock immediately with unsynchronized high-energy defibrillation because synchronization may fail. If recurrent TdP with long QT, give magnesium, address bradycardia/QT drivers, and ask for expert help for overdrive pacing or isoproterenol.
QT prolongation more dangerous with slow HR

text:
EKG Analysis

Options: transcutaneous pacing (+sedation), transvenous pacing (requires line, expertise)

title: Case 5
text:
Teaching Points:

Complete heart block = AV dissociation.
Atropine is reasonable in unstable bradycardia, but do not wait on it when high-grade or infranodal block is likely. Prepare pacing/pressors and transvenous pacing early.
Always have pacing pads in place during rapid responses.

Transcutaneous pacing will require sedation

title: Case 5
text:
Case summary
Label: Complete heart block / unstable bradycardia.
Key issue: atropine is reasonable, but do not wait when high-grade block is likely; prepare pacing, pressors, and transvenous pacing early.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Escalation, disposition, and closure
Learners will practice:

Deciding what next care step the patient needs
Calling the right resource early
Naming disposition, follow-up, callback, and triggers
Ending a code with team check, family plan, and debrief

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
The core question
What next step does this patient need?
Ask:

What is the risk in the next 5 minutes?
What decision is needed now?
What resource or capability is missing?
Where should the next care step happen?
Who follows up until that step happens?

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
VA RRT case
Elderly man, immediately hypoxemic after transfusion.
RR 24. SpO2 82% on 2 L.
Now worsening: tripoding, accessory muscle use, 100% FiO2 face mask, SpO2 upper 80s.

Prompt: What do you say out loud now?

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Call resources early



Signal
Action




Oxygenation or airway failure
Code/anesthesia


ICU monitoring or drips
ICU


STEMI/cath physiology
Cath


Focal neuro deficit
Stroke


Shock, PE, VT storm, device question
Shock/PERT/TICU by site



Code risk: bed out/down, pads on, airway/CPR access clear.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Every rapid needs an endpoint
A rapid response should end with one of these:

code blue
ICU transfer
rarely, a procedure
stabilized on the floor
goals-of-care transition

Always hand off to the team assuming care.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Next-step plan
Try:

“Disposition is [ICU / floor / code / goals-of-care].”


“Follow-up is owned by [me / primary team].”


“The person for the nurse to call is [name/team].”


“Are there concerns we have not addressed?”

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
How long to continue?




BMJ IHCA cohort: favorable functional status by CPR duration.



30 min: stop/continue huddle.
Anchor, not rule.
Longer: witnessed/monitored, shockable/improving, reversible cause/bridge, ROSC signs.
Shorter: unwitnessed/unmonitored, unchanged asystole/PEA, no target/ROSC/bridge.
Guardrail: OHCA TOR rules do not automatically apply to IHCA.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
How to stop ACLS

Summarize: “[duration] CPR, persistent [rhythm], no ROSC, no remaining reversible intervention.”
Ask: “Anything we have not tried?”
Announce: “One final rhythm/pulse check; if unchanged, we stop CPR.”

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
After the event: assign tasks

Family update: [name]
Documentation/time: recorder
Attending/workflow: primary team
Debrief: [time/place]

What went well? What changes? Does anyone need support?

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Summary

Next step needs more? Call early.
Moving where? Name disposition.
Who follows up? Name owner and callback.
Ending how? Team check, family plan, debrief.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Working with nurse-led response teams
Align decisions, expertise, and plan in the first 60 seconds
Learners will practice:

Understanding why support was called
Adding resident medical synthesis
Addressing team concerns and constraints
Closing the loop

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Nurse/outreach teams are a resource
Nurses often already know trajectory, failed attempts, resource constraints, and what may happen next.
Residents add synthesis, orders, escalation, and disposition.
Goal: better decisions and a clear next step.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Case start
An RRT has been called for a deteriorating patient.
The bedside nurse and critical care outreach nurse are already in the room.
The patient is newly confused, tachypneic, and on escalating oxygen.
The charge nurse is helping bring resources to the bedside.
Prompt: What decisions do you need to make, and who can help?

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
section: Move 1: Understand why support was called
text:
Move 1: Understand why support was called
Ask the bedside and outreach nurses:

“What changed, what have you tried, and what made you call for more support?”

Listen for:

uncertainty
missing resources
clinical trajectory
plan execution

Then name the decision needed now.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 2: Add your medical synthesis
Residents add synthesis, orders, escalation, and disposition.
Critical care nurses add trajectory, bedside reality, and resource constraints.
Use the same structure:

“I think [problem] is the issue. I’m worried about [risk]. My plan is [plan].”

Then ask:

“What are we missing?”

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 3: Address the team’s concerns
Check whether the plan answers the concern that triggered the RRT:

Does this plan address what worried you enough to call the RRT?
What constraint still makes this hard to execute?
What would make us change disposition or call more help?

If care needs exceed floor resources, name disposition and escalation now.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 4: Close the loop
Check with the team, then name:

disposition
follow-up owner
callback person
trigger


“Before I leave, does this plan address the concerns that brought us here?”

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Common failure modes

Ignore work already done
Ask for chart review, not trajectory
Give a plan without follow-up
Leave without next step or trigger
Dismiss the concern that triggered the RRT
Miss team expertise or resource constraints

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Summary

Understand why support was called.
Add medical synthesis.
Address team concerns and constraints.
Close the loop on next step, follow-up, and trigger.
